blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 5 (Solids and Fluid Dynamics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define stress and strain and name their kinds. Explain tensile, volumetric and shear strain with their formulas, and define Young's modulus with its unit. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Stress: the force applied per unit area to produce a change in the shape, volume or length of a body.
Stress (σ) = Force (F)/Area (A) ... (5.1)
SI unit: N m⁻², named pascal (Pa). A stress that changes length is tensile stress, one that changes volume is volume stress, and one that changes shape is shear stress.

Strain: a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it.
(i) Tensile (or compressive) strain: in one dimension, the fractional change in length (Fig. 5.3a).
Strain (ε) = Change in length (ΔL)/Original length (L₀) ... (5.2)
Strain is a ratio of lengths, so it is dimensionless and has no units. It is tensile strain if due to tensile stress, compressive strain if due to compressive stress.
(ii) Volumetric strain: when the stress changes the volume, the change in volume per unit volume (Fig. 5.3b).
Volumetric strain = ΔV/V₀ ... (5.3)
(iii) Shear strain: if y is the distance between two opposite faces and one face slides through Δx under shear stress (Fig. 5.3c),
γ = Δx/y = tan θ ... (5.4)
For a small angle θ in radian, tan θ ≅ θ, so γ = θ ... (5.5)

Young's modulus: the stress applied per unit strain.
Y = Tensile stress/Tensile strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L₀) ... (5.6)
It has the same unit as stress, N m⁻² or Pa. Values for some materials are given in Table 5.1 (e.g. steel 200 × 10⁹ N m⁻², copper 110 × 10⁹ N m⁻²).

book_ref.quote: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it.

blocks.prompt: 2 A wire 2.0 m long with cross-sectional area 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² stretches by 2.0 mm under a load of 160 N. Find (i) the stress (ii) the strain (iii) the Young's modulus of the material. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Stress = F/A, strain = ΔL/L₀, and Y is their ratio.

book_ref.quote: It has the same unit as that of stress i.e., N m⁻² or Pa.

blocks.final_answer: Stress = 2.0 × 10⁸ N m⁻², strain = 1.0 × 10⁻³, Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻²

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe Searle's method for determining the Young's modulus of a wire: the apparatus, the procedure and how Y is obtained from the graph. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Apparatus (Fig. 5.4): Two wires, an auxiliary (reference) wire and a test (experimental) wire, of equal lengths, of the same material and same diameter, hang from a rigid support. Their lower ends are connected to horizontal bars (frames F₁ and F₂). A constant weight hangs from the hook of the reference wire's bar and a hanger from the test wire, so that the wires remain stretched and free from kinks. A spirit level and a micrometer connect the two frames.

Procedure:
1. Measure the initial length L₀ of the wire with a metre scale.
2. Measure the diameter d with a screw gauge at several points along the wire and take the average.
3. Adjust the spirit level to the horizontal by turning the micrometer; record this reference reading.
4. Load the test wire with a further weight; the spirit level tilts due to elongation of the test wire.
5. Turn the micrometer screw to restore the spirit level to horizontal. Subtract the first reading from the second to get the extension ΔL.
6. Calculate stress and strain:
Stress = Weight/Area of wire = F/A = mg/πr²
Strain = ΔL/L₀ = Change in length/Original length
7. Repeat with increasing loads to get more values of stress and strain.
8. Plot stress against strain; the graph should be a straight line. Its slope is equal to the Young's modulus Y of the wire.

book_ref.quote: Experimentally, the magnitude of Young's modulus for a material in the form of wire can be found out

blocks.prompt: 4 In a Searle's experiment, a wire of original length 2.5 m and radius 0.50 mm extends by 1.25 mm when a mass of 4.0 kg is added. Find the stress, the strain and the Young's modulus. (Take π = 3.14.) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Stress = mg/πr², strain = ΔL/L₀; Y = stress/strain.

book_ref.quote: Repeat the above steps by increasing load on test wire to obtain more values of stresses and strains.

blocks.final_answer: Stress ≈ 5.0 × 10⁷ N m⁻², strain = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, Y ≈ 1.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻²

blocks.prompt: 5 Draw and explain the stress-strain curve of a ductile material. Explain proportional limit, elastic limit (yield point), plastic deformation, ultimate tensile strength and fracture. Also define ductile and brittle substances. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Tensile test: a metal wire is extended at a specified rate in a mechanical testing machine; the stresses are measured by an electronic device and the stress-strain curve is plotted automatically on an X-Y chart recorder (Fig. 5.5).

Region OA, proportional limit: In the initial stage, stress increases linearly with strain up to point A, the proportional limit σₚ: the greatest stress a material can endure without losing straight-line proportionality between stress and strain. Hooke's law (strain directly proportional to stress) is obeyed in OA. From A to B, stress and strain are not proportional.

Elastic limit (yield point B): If the load is removed at any point between O and B, the curve is retraced and the material returns to its original length. In region OB the material is elastic. B is the yield point and the stress at B is the elastic limit σₑ.

Plastic deformation: If the stress is increased beyond the elastic limit, the specimen is permanently changed and does not recover its original shape or size when the stress is removed. This is plasticity, the portion B to C.

Ultimate tensile strength (C): the maximum stress σᵤ a material can withstand; the nominal strength of the material.
Fracture (D): once C is crossed, the material breaks at D, the fracture stress σf.

Ductile substances undergo plastic deformation until they break, e.g. lead, copper, wrought iron.
Brittle substances break just after the elastic limit is reached, e.g. glass, high carbon steel; beryllium, bismuth and chromium are brittle metals.

book_ref.quote: A typical stress-strain curve for a ductile material is shown in Fig. 5.5.

blocks.prompt: 6 A copper wire of diameter 2.0 mm and length 1.5 m carries a load of 300 N. Assuming it stays in the region OA, find (i) the stress (ii) the strain (iii) the extension. Take Y for copper = 110 × 10⁹ N m⁻² (Table 5.1) and π = 3.14. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: In region OA Hooke's law holds, so strain = stress/Y; then ΔL = strain × L₀.

book_ref.quote: Hooke's law which states that the strain (deformation) is directly proportional to stress

blocks.final_answer: Stress = 9.55 × 10⁷ N m⁻², strain = 8.7 × 10⁻⁴, extension = 1.3 mm

blocks.prompt: 7 What is strain energy? Derive an expression for the energy stored in a stretched spring, and show that the strain energy per unit volume of a stretched material is ½ × stress × strain = ½Y(ΔL/L)². (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Strain energy: When a body is deformed by a force, work is done against the elastic restoring force. This work is stored in the body as potential energy, equal to the gain in P.E. of its molecules displaced from their mean positions.

Energy in a stretched spring: A spring is stretched by a force F through extension Δx (Fig. 5.6). Within the elastic limit the extension is directly proportional to the force, so the force increases uniformly from zero to F (Fig. 5.7). The average force is ½F.
Work done = Average force × Distance in the direction of the force
W = ½F × Δx ... (5.7)
From Hooke's law F = kΔx, therefore
W = (½kΔx)(Δx) = ½kΔx²
W = Area of triangle OPQ under the force-extension graph.
This work is stored as strain energy: E = ½F.Δx = ½kΔx²

Per unit volume: For a material of cross-sectional area A, length L and extension ΔL, the volume is AL. So
U = ½ × (F × ΔL)/(A × L)
U = ½ × (F/A) × (ΔL/L) ... (5.8)
U = ½ × stress × strain ... (5.9)
From Eq. (5.6), F/A = Y × (ΔL/L). Putting this in Eq. (5.8):
U = ½Y × (ΔL/L) × (ΔL/L) = ½Y(ΔL/L)² ... (5.10)
This equation gives the strain energy stored per unit volume of a stressed material.

book_ref.quote: Consider a material in the form of a spring as shown in Fig. 5.6.

blocks.prompt: 8 A steel wire (Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻²) of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² is stretched by a force of 100 N. Find (i) the extension (ii) the strain energy stored (iii) the strain energy per unit volume. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ΔL from Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L); energy = ½FΔL; divide by volume AL.

book_ref.quote: then the volume of the material will be AL

steps: Check: ½ × stress × strain = ½ × 1.0 × 10⁸ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.5 × 10⁴ J m⁻³

blocks.prompt: 9 State Archimedes' principle. Derive an expression for the upthrust on a solid cylinder immersed in a liquid and show that it equals the weight of the liquid displaced. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Upthrust: an upward force acts on an object kept inside a liquid, causing an apparent loss of weight; this force is the upthrust of the liquid.

Archimedes' principle: When an object is totally or partially immersed in a liquid, an upthrust force acts on it equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.

Derivation: Consider a solid cylinder of cross-sectional area A and height h immersed in a liquid of density ρ (Fig. 5.8). Let h₁ and h₂ be the depths of its top and bottom faces. Then
h₂ − h₁ = h ... (5.11)
Liquid pressures at these depths:
P₁ = ρgh₁ and P₂ = ρgh₂
Forces on the top and bottom faces:
F₁ = P₁A = ρgh₁A and F₂ = P₂A = ρgh₂A
F₁ and F₂ act on opposite faces, so the net force (the upthrust) is their difference:
F₂ − F₁ = ρgh₂A − ρgh₁A = ρgA(h₂ − h₁) ... (5.12)
Upthrust of liquid = ρgAh
Upthrust = ρgV ... (5.13)
Here Ah is the volume V of the cylinder, equal to the volume of liquid displaced; so ρgV is the weight of the liquid displaced. Thus the upthrust equals the weight of the liquid displaced, which is Archimedes' principle.

book_ref.quote: Consider a solid cylinder of cross-sectional area A and height h immersed in a liquid

blocks.prompt: 10 An empty balloon weighs 60 N and is filled with 15 m³ of hydrogen (density 0.09 kg m⁻³). The density of air is 1.3 kg m⁻³. Find the maximum load it can lift besides its own weight. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Upthrust = weight of air displaced; it must equal balloon + hydrogen + load.

book_ref.quote: How much maximum contents the balloon can lift besides its own weight?

steps: Weight of hydrogen w₁ = ρ_H Vg = 0.09 × 15 × 9.8 = 13.23 N

blocks.prompt: 11 State the principle of floatation. When does an object float or sink? Explain how floatation is used in ships, a wooden block, a hot-air balloon and a submarine. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Sinking and floating: An object sinks if its weight is greater than the upthrust on it. It floats if its weight is equal to or less than the upthrust. When it floats, the upthrust equals its weight, and it may be partially immersed. The upthrust is always equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.

Principle of floatation: A floating object displaces a fluid having weight equal to the weight of the object.
Archimedes' principle applies to liquids as well as gases.

Applications:
1. Hot-air balloon: its density is less than the surrounding air; when the buoyant force is more than its weight it rises. This is controlled by varying the quantity of hot air.
2. Wooden block: it floats because the weight of an equal volume of water is greater than the weight of the block; it sinks only until the displaced water equals its weight.
3. Ships and boats: designed on the principle of floatation; a ship would sink if its weight including passengers and goods became greater than the upthrust of water.
4. Submarine: it floats when the weight of water equal to its volume is greater than its weight. It has tanks that can be filled with or emptied of seawater. Filling them increases its weight; when weight exceeds upthrust it dives. To come up, the tanks are emptied.

book_ref.quote: This is the principle of floatation. It states that:

blocks.prompt: 12 A wooden block of volume 1.0 × 10⁻² m³ and mass 6.0 kg floats on water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). Find (i) the upthrust on it (ii) the volume of the block under water (iii) the fraction of its volume immersed. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For a floating body upthrust = weight; the immersed volume is the volume of water displaced.

book_ref.quote: In case of floating object, the object may be partially immersed.

blocks.final_answer: Upthrust = 58.8 N; immersed volume = 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³; 0.60 (60%) of the block is under water

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain the terms streamline, steady flow and turbulent flow, and why two streamlines cannot cross. State the conditions of an ideal fluid. Define rate of flow and derive the formula rate of flow = Av. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Streamline (laminar) flow: the flow is streamline if every particle passing a particular point moves along exactly the same path as earlier particles. The smooth path followed is a streamline; it may be straight or curved, and the tangent at any point gives the direction of flow. If the velocity at points P, Q, R does not change with time, the flow is steady (Fig. 5.12). Two streamlines cannot cross each other.

Steady flow: if the overall flow pattern does not change with time; every particle follows the same flow line as the previous particle.

Turbulent flow: the irregular or unsteady flow of a fluid. Above a certain velocity the motion becomes unsteady and irregular, the velocity changes abruptly, and there are eddies and whirlpools; the paths of the particles keep changing (Fig. 5.13).

Ideal fluid: (1) non-viscous, no friction between adjacent layers; (2) incompressible, constant density; (3) steady motion.

Rate of flow: the volume of fluid passing through any section of a pipe per unit time.
Derivation: A fluid flows with velocity v through a pipe of cross-sectional area A (Fig. 5.14). In time t it covers a distance
ℓ = vt
Volume passing in time t = A × ℓ = Avt
Rate of flow = Volume/Time = Avt/t = Av
Rate of flow = Av ... (5.14)
SI unit: m³ s⁻¹ (sometimes L s⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: Let the velocity of the fluid be v and it flows through the pipe for time t

blocks.prompt: 14 Water flows at 2.0 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of internal radius 1.5 cm. Find (i) the rate of flow (ii) the time needed to fill a tank of 0.50 m³. (Take π = 3.14.) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rate of flow = Av; time = volume ÷ rate of flow.

book_ref.quote: The rate of flow of a fluid through a pipe is the volume of the fluid passing through any section of pipe per unit time.

blocks.final_answer: Rate of flow = 1.41 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹; time ≈ 354 s (about 5.9 min)

blocks.prompt: 15 Starting from the conservation of mass, derive the equation of continuity A₁v₁ρ₁ = A₂v₂ρ₂ for steady flow through a pipe of non-uniform cross-section, reduce it to A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ for an incompressible fluid, and use it to explain why squeezing a rubber pipe increases the flow velocity. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statement: The product of cross-sectional area of the pipe and the fluid speed (Av) at any point along the pipe is constant; this constant equals the volume flow per second (flow rate).
Av = Constant = Volume/time

Derivation: A fluid flows steadily through a pipe of non-uniform size (Fig. 5.15). In a short time Δt the fluid at the lower end (area A₁) moves a distance Δx₁ with velocity v₁:
Δx₁ = v₁Δt ... (5.15)
Volume entering at A₁: V = A₁Δx₁ = A₁v₁Δt
If ρ₁ is the density there, the mass entering is
Δm₁ = A₁v₁Δt × ρ₁
Similarly, the mass leaving through the upper end (area A₂, velocity v₂, density ρ₂) in the same time Δt is
Δm₂ = A₂v₂Δt × ρ₂
If the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, mass is conserved: the mass flowing in through A₁ equals the mass flowing out through A₂.
Δm₁ = Δm₂ ... (5.16)
A₁v₁Δt × ρ₁ = A₂v₂Δt × ρ₂
A₁v₁ρ₁ = A₂v₂ρ₂ ... (5.17)
This is the equation of continuity. For an incompressible fluid the density is constant (ρ₁ = ρ₂), so
A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ ... (5.18)

Meaning: in steady flow the rate of flow inward equals the rate of flow outward; this justifies the conservation of mass of the fluid flowing through a pipe. Where the pipe is narrower, the fluid moves faster.

Squeezing a rubber pipe: squeezing decreases the cross-sectional area (A₂ < A₁), so by A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ the velocity v₂ must increase to maintain the same flow rate (5.10).

book_ref.quote: Consider a fluid flowing through a pipe of non-uniform size.

blocks.prompt: 16 Water flows at 0.50 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of diameter 6.0 cm which narrows to 2.0 cm. Find (i) the speed in the narrow part (ii) the rate of flow. (Take π = 3.14.) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: A ∝ d², so v₂ = v₁(d₁/d₂)²; the rate of flow is A₁v₁ (the same everywhere).

book_ref.quote: From equation of continuity, the mass of water discharging per second through area A is

blocks.final_answer: v₂ = 4.5 m s⁻¹; rate of flow = 1.41 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 17 Using the work-energy principle, derive Bernoulli's equation for the steady flow of an ideal fluid through a pipe of varying cross-section and height. State the assumptions and write the equation in its general form. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bernoulli's equation relates the pressure of a moving fluid to its speed and height. Assumptions: the fluid is incompressible, non-viscous and flows steadily.

Consider the fluid flowing through a pipe in time t (Fig. 5.16). At the upper end: pressure P₁, area A₁, speed v₁, height h₁. At the lower end: P₂, A₂, v₂, h₂.

Work done: The force on the upper end is P₁A₁. Work done on the fluid by the fluid behind it, in moving it through Δx₁:
W₁ = F₁Δx₁ = P₁A₁Δx₁
At the lower end the work is done against the fluid force, so it is negative:
W₂ = −F₂Δx₂ = −P₂A₂Δx₂
Net work: W = W₁ + W₂ = P₁A₁Δx₁ − P₂A₂Δx₂ ... (5.19)
With Δx₁ = v₁t and Δx₂ = v₂t: W = P₁A₁v₁t − P₂A₂v₂t
From the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so A₁v₁t = A₂v₂t = V (volume). Hence
W = (P₁ − P₂)V ... (5.20)
With V = m/ρ: W = (P₁ − P₂)m/ρ ... (5.21)

Energy changes: part of this work changes the K.E. and part the gravitational P.E.:
ΔK.E. = ½mv₂² − ½mv₁² ... (5.22)
ΔP.E. = mgh₂ − mgh₁ ... (5.23)
By the law of conservation of energy:
(P₁ − P₂)m/ρ = ½mv₂² − ½mv₁² + mgh₂ − mgh₁ ... (5.24)
Rearranging (multiplying by ρ/m):
P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂
This is Bernoulli's equation, often written as
P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant

book_ref.quote: The force on the upper end of the fluid is P₁A₁ where P₁ is the pressure

blocks.prompt: 18 Water flows down a pipe. At the upper end (height 5.0 m) the pressure is 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the speed 1.5 m s⁻¹. At the lower end (height 0) the area is half the upper area. Find the speed and the pressure at the lower end. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Continuity gives v₂; Bernoulli's equation then gives P₂.

book_ref.quote: where h₁ and h₂ are the heights of the upper and lower ends respectively.

steps: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ with A₂ = A₁/2: v₂ = 2v₁ = 3.0 m s⁻¹
P₂ = P₁ + ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) + ρg(h₁ − h₂)

blocks.prompt: 19 Derive the Venturi relation P₁ − P₂ = ½ρv₂² from Bernoulli's equation, stating each approximation. What is a venturi meter used for, and what does the result tell about speed and pressure? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Set-up (Fig. 5.22): a fluid of density ρ flows through a pipe. A₁ is the area at the wide end and A₂ at the narrow portion; v₁ and v₂ are the speeds there. The pressures P₁ and P₂ are shown by the limbs of a manometer connected to the two portions.

Step 1 (horizontal pipe): The pipe is horizontal, so the average potential energy is the same at both places. Bernoulli's equation becomes
P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂²
P₁ − P₂ = ½ρv₂² − ½ρv₁²
P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) ... (5.25)
This shows that where the speed is high, the pressure is low (P + ½ρv² = constant).

Step 2 (continuity): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₁ = A₂v₂/A₁. Since A₂ < A₁, v₁ is small compared with v₂: the fluid is very slow in the wide portion. So v₁ can be neglected in Eq. (5.25):
P₁ − P₂ = ½ρv₂² ... (5.26)
This is the Venturi relation.

Use: it is used in the venturi meter, a device used to measure the speed of liquid flow. Measuring P₁ − P₂ with the manometer gives v₂ = √(2(P₁ − P₂)/ρ).

book_ref.quote: Consider a pipe within which a fluid of density ρ is flowing through different areas of cross-section

blocks.prompt: 20 The manometer of a venturi meter carrying water shows a pressure difference of 12.5 kPa. The area of the narrow part is 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². Using the Venturi relation, find (i) the speed of water in the narrow part (ii) the rate of flow. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rearrange P₁ − P₂ = ½ρv₂² for v₂, then rate of flow = A₂v₂.

book_ref.quote: Pressure P₁ and P₂ indicate the liquid pressure at both the portions by connecting the limbs of the manometer.

steps: (ii) Rate of flow = A₂v₂ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 5.0 = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: v₂ = 5.0 m s⁻¹; rate of flow = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ (1.5 L s⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 21 Derive Torricelli's theorem from Bernoulli's equation for a large tank with a small orifice, state the theorem, and explain what happens if the orifice is pointed upward. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Set-up (Fig. 5.23): a large tank of fluid has small orifices A and B. Point 1 is the top surface (height h₁, speed v₁, pressure P₁); point 2 is the orifice A (height h₂, efflux speed v₂, pressure P₂).

Approximation: the orifices are so small that the efflux speeds are much larger than the speed v₁ of the top surface, so v₁ ≈ 0.
Bernoulli's equation becomes:
P₁ + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂
Both the top surface and the orifice are open to the air: P₁ = P₂ = atmospheric pressure. Cancelling them:
ρgh₁ = ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂
½v₂² = g(h₁ − h₂)
v₂ = √(2g(h₁ − h₂)) ... (5.27)

Torricelli's theorem: The speed of efflux is equal to the velocity gained by the fluid in falling through the distance (h₁ − h₂) under the action of gravity.

Explanation: the efflux speed is the same as that of a ball falling through (h₁ − h₂). The top level moves down a little, and P.E. is transferred into K.E. of the efflux. If the orifice is pointed upward (at B in Fig. 5.23), this K.E. would let the liquid rise to the level of the water in the tank. In practice, viscous-energy losses alter the result to some extent.

book_ref.quote: A simple application of Bernoulli's equation is shown in Fig. 5.23.

blocks.prompt: 22 A large water tank has a small hole of area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² at 3.2 m below the water surface. Find (i) the speed of efflux (ii) the volume of water flowing out per second (iii) the height to which the jet would rise if the hole were turned upward (ignore viscous losses). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Torricelli gives v; volume per second = Av; an upward jet rises back to the tank level.

book_ref.quote: Since the orifices are so small, the efflux speeds v₂ and v₃ will be much larger

steps: (ii) Volume per second = Av = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 7.92 = 1.58 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹
(iii) h = v²/2g = 62.7/19.6 = 3.2 m, i.e. up to the level of the water in the tank
blocks.final_answer: v ≈ 7.9 m s⁻¹; 1.58 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹; the jet rises 3.2 m (to the tank level)

blocks.prompt: 23 Explain, using Bernoulli's principle, the working of (i) an aeroplane wing (ii) a filter pump (iii) a carburetor (iv) a paint sprayer or perfume atomizer (v) a tall chimney. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: a number of devices work by the pressure difference that results from changes in the speed of a fluid: where the speed is high, the pressure is low.

(i) Aeroplane wing: the wing deflects the air so that streamlines are closer together above it than below (Fig. 5.17). Where streamlines are closer the speed is faster, so air above travels faster and the pressure there is lower. The higher pressure below forces the wing upward: this is the lift.

(ii) Filter pump: it has a constriction in the centre, so the water jet from the tap flows faster there. This lowers the pressure near it, and air flows in from the side tube. Air and water are expelled together through the lower part (Fig. 5.19).

(iii) Carburetor: it uses a Venturi duct to feed the correct mixture of air and petrol to the cylinders. Air is drawn very fast through the duct, creating low pressure, which draws petrol vapours from a tiny side inlet into the air stream (Fig. 5.20).

(iv) Paint sprayer / perfume atomizer: squeezing the rubber ball blows air through a tube; it rushes out of a narrow aperture at high speed, causing a fall of pressure over a tube dipped in the liquid. Atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up into the air stream (Fig. 5.21).

(v) Chimney: a tall chimney exposed to air currents works best; the moving air reduces the pressure at the top and forces the upward flow of smoke.

book_ref.quote: A number of devices operate by means of pressure difference that results from changes in the speed of the fluid.

blocks.prompt: 24 Air (density 1.3 kg m⁻³) flows over the upper surface of an aeroplane wing at 70 m s⁻¹ and under the lower surface at 60 m s⁻¹. The wing area is 20 m². Treating the wing as thin and horizontal, find (i) the pressure difference (ii) the lift force. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For a horizontal flow P + ½ρv² = constant, so the lower (slower) side has the higher pressure; lift = ΔP × area.

book_ref.quote: the wing will be forced upward and the lift of an aeroplane is due to this effect

blocks.final_answer: Pressure difference = 845 Pa; lift ≈ 1.69 × 10⁴ N upward

blocks.prompt: 25 Explain viscous drag and state Stokes' law. Describe how a droplet falling through air reaches terminal velocity, and derive the expression vₜ = 2gr²ρ/9η. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Viscosity and drag: the frictional effect between layers of a flowing fluid is its viscosity; it measures how much force is needed to slide one layer of liquid over another (coefficient η). Since liquids and gases have non-zero viscosity, an object moving through them experiences a retarding force called the drag force, which increases as the speed of the object increases.

Stokes' law: the drag force F on a sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is
F = 6πηrv ... (5.28)
At high speeds the force is no longer simply proportional to speed.

Terminal velocity: a water droplet (e.g. of fog) falling vertically first accelerates rapidly under gravity. As its speed increases, the upward drag increases. The net force is
Net force = Weight − Drag force ... (5.29)
Finally the drag becomes equal to the weight; the net force is zero and the droplet falls with a constant speed called the terminal velocity vₜ.

Derivation: using Stokes' law for the drag and equating it to the weight:
0 = mg − 6πηrvₜ
vₜ = mg/6πηr ... (5.30)
The mass of the droplet is m = ρV, where V = (4/3)πr³. So
vₜ = (4/3)πr³ρg/6πηr
vₜ = 2gr²ρ/9η ... (5.31)
Thus the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius.

book_ref.quote: Consider a water droplet such as that of fog falling vertically

blocks.prompt: 26 A water droplet of radius 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m falls through air (η = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹, ρ of water = 1000 kg m⁻³). Find (i) its terminal velocity (ii) the drag force on it at terminal velocity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use vₜ = 2gr²ρ/9η; at terminal velocity the drag equals the weight.

book_ref.quote: Equating it to the weight of the drop, we have

blocks.final_answer: vₜ ≈ 0.29 m s⁻¹; drag at terminal velocity ≈ 5.1 × 10⁻⁹ N
